_comment: NEUTRAL EXAMPLE — the engine ships with no operator patterns on purpose.
Copy to guardrail-patterns.json (gitignored) and edit, or have your private
<org>-instance overlay place that file here. The router mounts ./context
read-only, so this directory is how config reaches it — the same slot
brand.md and hygiene.json already use.
WHY THIS EXISTS. router/guardrails.js ships a default pattern set in a
public repo, so anyone can read it. For the OUTPUT patterns that is fine:
they match vendor credential FORMATS the vendors publish themselves, and
every open scanner uses the same ones. The INPUT (prompt-injection) patterns
are different — those phrasings are the defender's own work, and an attacker
who reads the regex can phrase around it immediately. Patterns you add here
never appear in the public repo, so a reader of the engine learns the
defaults, not yours.
This is defence in depth, NOT the boundary. The real isolation guarantee is
structural: per-scope mounts, per-scope tool allowlists, firewalled runners,
human gates. Anyone who can probe a running deployment can map a detection
layer empirically in a few dozen requests, so treat these as tripwires that
raise cost and produce audit signal — never as the wall.
SCHEMA. mode: 'extend' (default, adds to the built-ins) or 'replace'
(swaps the built-in set for yours, per section). Entries:
{ type, level: low|medium|high, re: <JS regex source>, flags: 'imsu' }.
Flags g and y are refused: scan() reads match[0] and those break it.
An invalid regex is dropped with a warning, never silently — and a
malformed file keeps the built-ins rather than disabling the control.
CAUTION. These regexes run on every prompt and every runner result. A
catastrophically backtracking pattern will stall the router; test anything
with nested quantifiers against a long adversarial input before shipping it.
